Therefore, to ensure broad representation across relevant clinical specialties, healthcare settings, and geographic regions, while maintaining informed and consistent participation across Delphi rounds, the aim was for a panel of 35–40 experts. Quality metrics and conceptual framework The definition used for quality metrics was the Donabedian framework used by the Agency of Healthcare Quality and Research . Quality metrics thereby refer to measures used to assess the clinical performance, care quality, and safety measures of healthcare providers (hospitals or physicians). The final set of metrics was organized using the Donabedian framework, which suggests that improvements in structure of care lead to improvements in processes of care, which lead to improvements in outcomes. Structure of care refers to the characteristics of where the care occurs (‘What are the organizational resources to care for the patient?’); process of care consists of clinical processes performed in the healthcare setting (‘What is done to the patient?’); and outcomes identify the ultimate status of the patient following the care (‘What happens to the patient?’) , . Delphi rounds Delphi rounds were self-administered online using SurveyMonkey (SurveyMonkey, San Mateo, CA, USA). Emails including individual links were sent to each participant. The panellists had 3 weeks to complete each survey. Non-responders were sent reminders at 1 and 2 weeks after the initial invitation. Round 1 aimed to generate an exhaustive list of quality of metrics for the use of perioperative RBCT in GI cancer surgery for structures, processes, and outcomes of care. Open-ended questions were used, asking ‘Which metrics should be used to evaluate quality (or appropriate) utilization of perioperative RBCTs in GI cancer surgery?’. Rounds 2 and 3 aimed to reach consensus on the list of most relevant quality metrics. In Round 2, a web-based survey presented the list of quality metrics identified in Round 1. Panellists were asked to rate (dis)agreement with the importance of each item using a six-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not important at all) to 5 (very important). In Round 3, the panellists were asked to re-rate the items for which consensus was not reached during the previous round. For each round, participants were able to suggest editing to the quality metrics listed and provide comments regarding the rationale for their scoring. In the final round, the metrics for which consensus had been established in previous rounds were presented and panellists were asked to rank them from most important to least important in each domain. Panellists were also asked to rate the feasibility of measuring each metric for monitoring in their care environment using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (very feasible) to 5 (not feasible at all). The final list of quality metrics comprised metrics that were highly ranked and had a median feasibility rating of 1 or 2. If two included metrics measured the same construct, they were combined. A final face-to-face or virtual consensus meeting was not planned because this is not always required when consensus is predefined using quantitative criteria and response stability is achieved across rounds. Given convergence of ratings, the absence of new domains after item generation, and the lack of polarized subgroup disagreement, a fully iterative Delphi process was considered methodologically preferable. Indeed, when the objective is selection and prioritization, iterative rating alone is considered sufficient . Moreover, for large, geographically distributed panels, meetings can disproportionately privilege more vocal or centrally located participants; fully remote Delphi processes are appropriate and increasingly standard in such contexts , . Analysis Anonymized results were analysed if the response rate for the round was > 75% of panellists. The median score for each item and the number of panellists per rating level were computed. Consensus was defined following University of California, Los Angeles–Research and Development (RAND/UCLA) recommendations , adapted to the Likert scale used in this study. The RAND/UCLA methods evaluate agreement (importance) and consensus based on the median and distribution of ordinal ratings rather than simple percentages of agreement. This approach preserves information on the strength, dispersion, and polarization of expert judgments, and provides a more robust and interpretable assessment of consensus than binary percentage-based thresholds , . Importance was defined by collapsing answers into three categories: important (rating 4–5 on the Likert scale), neutral (rating 2–3 on the Likert scale), and not important (rating 0–1 on the Likert scale). Consensus was defined as ≤ 22 panellists rating outside the score category containing the median. Lack of consensus was defined as ≥ 22 panellists rating in each extreme score category (0–1 or 4–5). If neither of those criteria was satisfied, agreement

Histograms were visually inspected and checked for bimodal distribution of the scores for each statement. Analyses were performed using R v4.1.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Results Panellists The final panel included 37 panellists from 13 countries (25 surgeons, 8 anaesthetists, and 4 transfusion medicine specialists; ). The characteristics of the panellists are presented in . Delphi rounds Four rounds of web-based anonymous Delphi survey were completed. The response rate was 78.4% for Round 1 (29 of 37), 86.5% (31 of 37) for Round 2, 88.9% (32 of 37) for Round 3, and 75.7% (28 of 37) for Round 4. Score distributions were unimodal across all rounds. During Round 1, items to address in the statements were listed by the panellists and categorized by domains of the Donabedian framework of process (care delivery), outcomes, and structures of care. An additional category of metrics as created to include suggested items of equity in RBCT use, patient-reported outcomes, patient satisfaction, and patient quality of life. In all, 72 possible metrics were presented for subsequent ratings during Rounds 2 and 3. During Round 2, 36 metrics reached consensus for importance. Of the items without consensus, one was considered of uncertain importance, and the remainder were of indeterminate importance. These items were presented again for rating in Round 3, with all then being rated as indeterminate. The details of Rounds 2 and 3 are presented in . In Round 4, all metrics that had reached consensus and rated as important were presented for relative ranking of importance and for scoring of feasibility. The results are presented in . Of the 36 quality metrics presented, 20 were included. Metrics capturing RBCT for haemoglobin >7 g/dl were combined into a single metric. Mean surgical service RBCT rate and mean institution RBCT rate were included under the metric of rate of perioperative RBCT with a specification to measure and monitor that metric at the service and institutional levels. Patient-reported outcomes were incorporated in the outcome domain. Final set of quality metrics Ultimately, five quality metrics are recommended for process (care delivery), four are recommended for outcomes, and eight are recommended for structures of care. One additional quality metric of patient-reported outcome is recommended for assessment of patient experience. The final set of recommended quality metrics is summarized within the Donabedian framework in . Process and outcomes quality metrics can be measured and monitored. Structure of care metrics are conceptualized as a checklist of characteristics of care that the hospital should have to provide quality care in perioperative RBCT ( ). Discussion With this international modified Delphi consensus process, quality metrics were defined to evaluate the use of perioperative RBCT for GI cancer surgery. This work focused on GI cancer surgery because this is a population at particularly high risk for RBCT and its repercussions owing to the combination of frequent preoperative anaemia and the need for major surgery. Using a structured, four-round process grounded in the Donabedian framework, 18 quality metrics were identified and prioritized across domains of process, outcomes, and structures of care. These metrics reflect both clinical relevance and feasibility for quality monitoring. This was an important step to address the lack of standardized tools to assess perioperative transfusion for quality improvement. Previous studies on perioperative RBCT have focused on its association with downstream outcomes such as surgical site infection, morbidity, mortality, length of hospital stay, and cancer survival , , . Despite growing evidence and consensus recommendations for both postoperative and intraoperative RBCT use, significant variation exists in the use of perioperative RBCT , , . Previous studies using population-based data from over 59 000 patients demonstrated that this variation is largely driven by treating physicians and hospitals . That variation was associated with increased rates of postoperative major morbidity and mortality; for example, every 10% increase in physician-level RBCT rates was linked to a 3.8% increase in major morbidity and a 0.3% increase in mortality . That variation was associated with increased rates of postoperative major morbidity and mortality; for example, every 10% increase in physician-level RBCT rates was linked to a 3.8% increase in major morbidity and a 0.3% increase in mortality . This represents a form of unwarranted variation, which is variation in care that is not attributable to patient need but rather to the quality, appropriateness, and efficiency of care often related to physician and institutional preferences , . Reducing such variation is crucial to minimizing unnecessary RBCT for the benefit of patients and health systems alike. Although patient-level transfusion risk factors may be difficult to modify, care at the individual provider and hospital levels are modifiable targets for intervention. The present study is an important first step to address practice at those levels by defining quality metrics that can allow institutions and clinicians to systematically and reproducibly audit and monitor RBCT use. Monitoring of quality in RBCT has traditionally focused on audits of transfusion reactions and blood bank management , . Although overall tracking of transfusion rates has been reported for quality improvement at some institutions , such initiatives have been limited by a single metric and have not considered the unique perioperative context specifically. Until now, there have been no standardized quality metrics to guide performance feedback and support sustainable improvements. The quality metrics developed in the present study aim to support hospital- and system-level strategies to minimize unwarranted variation in perioperative RBCT for GI cancer surgery. There are three main types of quality metrics, all built around the Donabedian framework: structure, process, and outcome metrics . There is debate over the relative value of these types of metrics. Process metrics are generally easier to interpret and act upon but only reflect quality if they are associated with the ultimate desirable outcomes . Outcome metrics do not reflect the care as directly, but are powerful in high-volume settings and can assess the downstream effect of care processes . Ultimately, a combination of different metrics is most often needed. The metrics identified through the modified Delphi process in the present study combine all three types of metrics to provide a comprehensive toolset for assessment and monitoring of perioperative RBCT practices. Importantly, feasibility was assessed using a diverse international panel, ensuring relevance across different institutions, practice settings, and health system structures. Although the implementation of these metrics may vary, from institutional dashboards to system-level benchmarking, for example, the set of quality metrics proposed herein lays the groundwork for quality improvement in perioperative RBCT for GI cancer surgery. The final set of quality metrics proposed reflects the principle of meaningful, feasible, and actionable measurement across process, outcome, and structure. The selected process metrics, including overall perioperative RBCT rates (stratified into intraoperative (day of surgery) and postoperative (days 1–3) periods), have been previously associated with adverse outcomes and thus represent outcome-validated measures of quality , , . Previous studies have confirmed that the rate of RBCT is also able to detect variation between providers, both physicians and hospitals, which is a key characteristic of a good quality metric , . Of note, broader windows were considered for the capture of RBCT, including 30 and 90 days, and ultimately the 3-day period was prioritized by the expert panel. This is consistent with the transfusion variable captured in the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program of the American College of Surgeons . The metric on RBCT administration for haemoglobin levels > 7 g/dl highlights potentially avoidable transfusions and serves as target for quality improvement. Outcome metrics of 30-day major morbidity, mortality, and transfusion reactions capture the impact of transfusion practices, whereas patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) underscore the importance of integrating patient perspectives into quality assessment. Indeed, recent patient interviews have highlighted opportunities to better align perioperative RBCT decisions with patient preferences . However, further work is needed to define optimal PROMs to use and how to capture them. To this end, potentially relevant PROM domains include postoperative fatigue, functional recovery, symptom burden, and health-related quality of life. Finally, structure metrics proposed include key enablers of safe transfusion practices: on-site blood banks, perioperative transfusion protocols, patient blood management programmes, and protocols for massive transfusion, anticoagulation reversal, and perioperative indications for RBCT. These elements are necessary to support adherence to evidence-based transfusion thresholds and minimize transfusion-related harm. It is acknowledged that quality metrics are only one component of the complex process of quality monitoring , . PROM domains include postoperative fatigue, functional recovery, symptom burden, and health-related quality of life. Finally, structure metrics proposed include key enablers of safe transfusion practices: on-site blood banks, perioperative transfusion protocols, patient blood management programmes, and protocols for massive transfusion, anticoagulation reversal, and perioperative indications for RBCT. These elements are necessary to support adherence to evidence-based transfusion thresholds and minimize transfusion-related harm. It is acknowledged that quality metrics are only one component of the complex process of quality monitoring , . Many more factors play a role in improving outcomes and cannot all be addressed in the scope of this project. Additional work using other methods will eventually be needed, including the development of benchmarks and implementation strategies adapted to local contexts, as well as considerations of equity in quality monitoring. This work has limitations. First, the final set of recommended quality metrics relies on expert consensus methodology, owing to the lack of direct empirical evidence on quality metrics for perioperative RBCT. The quality metrics proposed were based on expert judgment, clinical experience, and interpretation of established relationships between RBCT practices and outcomes from existing literature. Nonetheless, this work provides an important first step towards defining and standardizing quality metrics for RBCT. The reliability of the process was strengthened by a high number of panellists and survey rounds, with 37 international multidisciplinary experts, representation across 13 countries, and a > 75% response rate to each survey round , . Second, the breadth of possible quality metrics for RBCT is vast and, to create a parsimonious set of metrics, only the most relevant ones could be retained. As a result, the metrics that did not reach consensus for importance were discarded after Round 3, even though they may not have reached consensus for being ‘not important’. In addition, although the initial list of candidate metrics was generated through open-ended input from a large, multidisciplinary international Delphi panel, there remains a theoretical risk that some relevant metrics were not captured. Several features of the process support that conceptual saturation was likely achieved, including substantial thematic redundancy across Round 1 submissions and the absence of new domains or fundamentally new metrics emerging in subsequent rounds despite opportunities for panellists to suggest additional items. Nevertheless, some potentially relevant metrics may have been excluded. Finally, this work focused on GI cancer surgery, for reasons previously outlined, but the principles and metrics proposed may hold relevance in other surgical contexts where minimizing unnecessary RBCT remains a shared goal. Chou2 Department of Pathology and Lab Medicine, Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, and 1 Department of Pediatrics, Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, PA, USA 2 ABSTRACT Haematologica 2021 R ed cell transfusion remains a critical component of care for acute Volume 106(7):1805-1815 and chronic complications of sickle cell disease. Randomized clin- ical trials demonstrated the benefits of transfusion therapy for prevention of primary and secondary strokes and postoperative acute chest syndrome. Transfusion for splenic sequestration, acute chest syn- drome, and acute stroke are guided by expert consensus recommenda- tions. Despite overall improvements in blood inventory safety, adverse effects of transfusion are prevalent among patients with sickle cell dis- ease and include alloimmunization, acute and delayed hemolytic trans- fusion reactions, and iron overload. Judicious use of red cell transfu- sions, optimization of red cell antigen matching, and the use of erythro- cytapheresis and iron chelation can minimize adverse effects. Early recognition and management of hemolytic transfusion reactions can avert poor clinical outcomes. In this review, we discuss transfusion methods, indications, and complications in sickle cell disease with an emphasis on alloimmunization. Introduction Transfusion remains a central intervention for sickle cell disease (SCD), with most patients receiving one or more transfusions by adulthood.1 Prospective, ran- domized clinical trials support transfusion for primary and secondary stroke pre- vention, but for many other indications, treatment is based on expert consensus. Travis Lau, MD***** Bleeding after cardiac surgery is a common and serious complication leading to transfusion of mul- tiple blood products and resulting in increased morbidity and mortality. Despite the publication of numerous guidelines and consensus statements for patient blood management in cardiac surgery, research has revealed that adherence to these guidelines is poor, and as a result, a significant variability in patient transfusion practices among practitioners still remains. In addition, although utilization of point-of-care (POC) coagulation monitors and the use of novel therapeutic strategies for perioperative hemostasis, such as the use of coagulation factor concentrates, have increased significantly over the last decade, they are still not widely available in every institution. Therefore, despite continuous efforts, blood transfusion in cardiac surgery has only modestly declined over the last decade, remaining at ≥50% in high-risk patients. Given these limitations, and in response to new regulatory and legislature requirements, the Society of Cardiovascular Anesthesiologists (SCA) has formed the Blood Conservation in Cardiac Surgery Working Group to organize, summa- rize, and disseminate the available best-practice knowledge in patient blood management in car- diac surgery. The current publication includes the summary statements and algorithms designed by the working group, after collection and review of the existing guidelines, consensus statements, and recommendations for patient blood management practices in cardiac surgery patients. The overall goal is creating a dynamic resource of easily accessible educational material that will help to increase and improve compliance with the existing evidence-based best practices of patient blood management by cardiac surgery care teams. Transfusion thresholds for guiding red blood cell transfusion 2021 12 21 12 2021 CD002042 The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 10.1002/14651858.CD002042.pub5 PMC8691808 34932836 Abstract Background The optimal haemoglobin threshold for use of red blood cell (RBC) transfusions in anaemic patients remains an active area of research. Blood is a limited resource, and there are concerns about risks, including transmitted infections. If a liberal transfusion strategy does not improve clinical outcomes, or if it is equivalent, then adopting a more restrictive approach should be recognised as the standard of care. Objectives The aim of this review update was to compare 30‐day mortality and other clinical outcomes for participants randomised to restrictive versus liberal red blood cell (RBC) transfusion thresholds (triggers) for all clinical conditions. The restrictive transfusion threshold uses a lower haemoglobin concentration as a threshold for transfusion (most commonly, 7.0 g/dL to 8.0 g/dL), and the liberal transfusion threshold uses a higher haemoglobin concentration to direct transfusion (most commonly, 9.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL). Increasingly, investigators are considering other strategies including physiological triggers (i.e. central venous oxygen saturation), alone or in combination with such thresholds, to determine when a transfusion is indicated, so it is important to assess this growing body of evidence in tandem. We checked reference lists of published reviews and papers for additional trials. We included 61 trials (27,639 participants), across a range of clinical contexts: orthopaedic, cardiac or vascular surgery; critical care; neurocritical care; gastrointestinal bleeding; trauma; acute myocardial infarction; haematological malignancies and postpartum haemorrhage. The haemoglobin concentration used to define the restrictive transfusion group in most trials was between 7.0 g/dL and 8.0 g/dL. The main outcomes were exposure to blood transfusion, 30‐day mortality, neurologic function, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, cerebral vascular accident, infection and thromboembolism. Studies were generally at low risk of bias. Restrictive transfusion strategies reduced the risk of receiving at least one RBC transfusion by 42% when combining all clinical contexts (risk ratio (RR) 0.58, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.52 to 0.65; high‐certainty evidence), with a large amount of heterogeneity between trials (I² = 97%), reflecting diversity in the strength of estimates, not the efficacy of the policy. When combining all clinical contexts, restrictive transfusion strategies did not modify the risk of 30‐day mortality compared with liberal transfusion strategies (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.14; 44 studies, 22,575 participants; high‐certainty evidence) or any of the other outcomes assessed including myocardial infarction, stroke, thromboembolism or infection (moderate to high‐certainty evidence). There were two exceptions in clinical populations. In gastrointestinal bleeding, 30‐day mortality was lower with a restrictive transfusion strategy (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95; 4 studies, 1574 participants). In critically ill patients with brain injury, unfavourable neurological outcome at 6 to 12 months was lower with a liberal transfusion strategy (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.22; 4 studies, 2297 participants) (moderate‐certainty evidence). Transfusion‐specific reactions are uncommon, but occurred more frequently with the liberal strategy (Peto odds ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.62; 18 studies, 11,505 participants). Paediatric threshold comparison We included eight trials (2764 participants), across a limited range of clinical contexts (critical care, cardiac surgery, haematological malignancies and severe malarial anaemia). The haemoglobin concentration used to define the restrictive group in critical care and haematological malignancies trials was between 6.5 g/dL and 8.0 g/dL, and between 7.0 g/dL and 9 g/dL in cardiac surgery trials, depending on the cardiac abnormality and stage of repair. Studies were generally at low risk of bias. There was no clear difference in 30‐day mortality between restrictive and liberal transfusion strategies, although confidence intervals were wide (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.72 to 2.08; 7 studies, 2571 participants; low‐certainty evidence). There was moderate‐certainty evidence of no clear difference between threshold strategies for infection; very low‐certainty evidence of little to no difference for thrombosis and very low‐certainty evidence of little to no difference for the outcomes multiple organ dysfunction and cerebrovascular accident. Physiological triggers Nine trials in adults (3818 participants) and one trial in children (100 participants) were identified. These tested different interventions and measures of physiological parameters in diverse clinical populations. The risk of bias was variable. Meta‐analysis was not appropriate due to heterogeneity. Authors' conclusions A restrictive transfusion strategy significantly decreased the proportion of adults and children exposed to RBC transfusion. In most clinical contexts, there was no evidence of harm from a restrictive compared with a liberal transfusion strategy. Neurocritically ill patients, however, have better neurological outcomes at 6 to 12 months with a liberal transfusion strategy. Further work is needed to improve our understanding of outcomes beyond mortality, and to what degree the optimal strategies for transfusion should be modified in some patient populations, including different types of acute bleeding, cancers and subgroups of patients with myocardial infarction and other neurological injuries. New studies need to recognise the clinical context and the limitations of the adoption of a single threshold of haemoglobin, and to consider evaluating the use of physiological parameters to modify transfusion. Plain language summary Is it safe to use lower blood counts (haemoglobin levels) as a trigger for blood transfusion in order to give fewer blood transfusions? Key messages • The evidence suggests that waiting to give blood transfusions to most adults and children until their blood counts are lower (haemoglobin levels of 7.0 g/dL to 8.0 g/dL) compared to higher blood counts (9.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL) does not lead to higher risks of death, heart attack, stroke, pneumonia, blood clots or infection. Giving less blood would reduce unnecessary transfusions, which have risks. • Some studies, rather than simply measuring haemoglobin levels, are testing other ways of deciding when a transfusion is necessary, but it is not possible to say which tests are better. • Adults with acute brain injury may have a better ability to walk or take care of themselves if given blood transfusion to maintain higher blood counts. More research is needed to improve our understanding of outcomes other than death, including quality of life, and to understand which people may benefit from transfusing at a higher haemoglobin count. What happens in people who need blood transfusions? Doctors and healthcare professionals often give blood transfusions to people with low blood counts (anaemia), for surgery, bleeding or illness, but transfusions should only be given when we know they help people. Blood is a limited resource and transfusion is not risk‐free, especially for people in low‐income countries where testing for viruses such as HIV or hepatitis may be less available. What did we want to find out? 'Blood count' measures the amount of haemoglobin in the blood. Haemoglobin is a protein that carries oxygen around the body. A normal blood count is at or above 12 grams a decilitre (12 g/dL). We wanted to find out if it is safe to withhold transfusions until the blood count drops to low thresholds, rather than transfusing at higher blood counts. What did we do? We examined the results of studies that allocated people to one of two groups by chance (for example, by flipping a coin). In one group, the participants only received blood transfusions if their blood count fell below a higher threshold (typically, 9.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL). In the other group, the participants only received transfusions if their blood count fell below a lower threshold (typically, 7.0 g/dL to 8.0 g/dL). (The ‘threshold’ is the blood count level that would need to be met before a transfusion would be given.) What did we find? We found 79 studies including 31,457 adults and 2864 children. Participants were undergoing treatment for different reasons including: bone (orthopaedic), heart (cardiac) or blood vessel surgery; critical care; bleeding in the stomach or intestines; heart diseases; blood cancers; brain injury and childbirth. Studies compared higher or lower blood count thresholds for giving blood transfusion. Transfusion We found that adults who received transfusions only at lower blood count thresholds were 42% less likely to receive a blood transfusion than those who received them only at higher blood count thresholds. Findings were similar for children, but the number of studies including children was much smaller. Death and harmful events Overall, there was no clear difference in the risk of dying within 30 days of receiving, or not receiving, a transfusion for most participants in the two different threshold groups, with the possible exception of people with gastrointestinal bleeding, where the risk of dying was lower with transfusion given at a lower threshold. There was also little to no difference between threshold groups for outcomes including the number of serious harmful events, such as infection, heart attacks, strokes and blood clots. We found that critically ill adults with acute brain injury had better recovery in the longer term (6 to 12 months) with a liberal transfusion strategy. What are the limitations of the evidence? Most studies provided high‐quality evidence; they were adequately conducted and used methods that minimised biases that could make the validity of the results uncertain. We are confident in the evidence regarding the likelihood of receiving a transfusion, death within 30 days of transfusion, heart attack, stroke and infection. We are moderately confident in the evidence for infections and for blood clots, but the number of events for blood clots was smaller. The number of studies varied between conditions, and more evidence is needed in some areas (e.g. blood cancer and vascular surgery). Almost half of the studies reported on quality of life, but it was difficult to compare trials and determine whether one strategy was better than the other. How up‐to‐date is this evidence? This is an update of work last published in 2021; 31 new studies are included. The evidence is up‐to‐date to October 2024.
